Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers moves each item as soon as it arrives. A producer writes a job, workers pull from the queue, and latency stays close to the time the work itself takes. Adding capacity means starting more workers. You pay for that in machinery. There is a broker to run, visibility timeouts to tune, retries and a dead-letter path, and handlers that tolerate being called twice, because a worker can die halfway through and the job comes back.

Scheduled batch runs collect work and process it on a clock. One process wakes at 02:00, reads everything that accumulated since the last run, and writes results in a single pass. Failure handling is cruder and therefore easier, since either the run finished or you run it again. Because you see the whole set at once, you can sort it, drop duplicates, and hit the database with a few large statements instead of ten thousand small ones, which usually costs far less per item.

Pick by how stale a result is allowed to be. Someone waiting on a password reset email will not wait until 02:00. A billing rollup gains nothing from per-event processing.

Most systems end up with both, using a queue for anything a person is watching and a nightly batch for aggregates, reconciliation, and cleanup of whatever the queue dropped.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

Failure in the queue model is per item. A worker that crashes or throws leaves the job unacknowledged, the visibility timeout expires, and the broker hands the same message to another worker. Everything else keeps flowing, so one bad record does not stall the other thousands. The cost is that you have to decide how many attempts are enough, back off between them so a failing downstream service is not hammered, and route the exhausted job somewhere a person will look. A dead-letter queue nobody reads is a silent data loss channel.

Failure in a batch run is per run. The 02:00 job dies at item 4,000 of 10,000 and you are left asking what it already wrote. If the pass is idempotent, or wrapped in one transaction, you rerun it and stop thinking about it. If it sends email or charges cards, the rerun duplicates everything before the crash unless each item records that it was handled. The other half of the problem is timing: the run fails at 02:00, nobody notices until morning, and by then the work has a full day of backlog behind it. Batch failures need an alert on the run itself, since there is no queue depth quietly climbing to tell you something broke.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

output:
For a team of three or four people, start with the batch run. A cron entry and a script that reads a table are things you can write in an afternoon and debug by rerunning them by hand. A queue adds a broker to operate, a worker fleet to deploy, and a class of bug that only shows up under a redelivery you cannot reproduce locally. Pay that when something concrete forces you to: a user waiting on the result, or a nightly run that no longer finishes before people arrive.

When you do reach for a queue, use one your database already gives you. Postgres with a jobs table, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and a worker loop covers a few thousand jobs a minute, keeps the job state in the same transaction as your data, and lets you look at the queue with the SQL you already know. Redis or SQS becomes worth the separate system somewhere past that, or when the workers need to scale independently of the database.

Write handlers so a repeat call is harmless from the first day, whichever you pick. That single habit is what lets you move a job from the batch script to the queue later without rewriting it, and it costs almost nothing while the code is still small.
